Remove the unit gaps and compare volumes

question: Real numbers \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z\) are chosen independently and at random from the interval \([0,n]\) for some positive integer \(n.\) The probability that no two of \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z\) are within \(1\) unit of each other is greater than \(\dfrac{1}{2}.\) What is the smallest possible value of \(n?\)
solution:
Ordering the three numbers lets us remove the two required unit gaps. If \(n\leq 2\), two consecutive gaps greater than \(1\) cannot fit in the interval, so the desired probability is zero. We therefore consider \(n>2\).

Independence and uniform sampling make \((x,y,z)\) a uniform point in the cube \([0,n]^3\). Thus the probability is the favorable volume divided by \(n^3\). Cases where two coordinates differ by exactly \(1\) lie on planes of zero volume, so including these boundary cases does not change the probability.

First consider the ordering \(x\leq y\leq z\). The required conditions are
\[0\leq x,\qquad x+1\leq y,\qquad y+1\leq z\leq n.\]
The first and last numbers are then automatically at least \(2\) units apart. To remove the two unit gaps, set
\[u=x,\qquad v=y-1,\qquad w=z-2.\]
The conditions become
\[0\leq u\leq v\leq w\leq n-2.\]
These fixed coordinate shifts translate the region and preserve its volume. Reversing the shifts restores the required gaps and keeps all three original numbers in \([0,n]\), so the correspondence works in both directions.

The cube \([0,n-2]^3\) splits into six regions according to the coordinate order. There are \(3\cdot2\cdot1=6\) orders, and permuting coordinates makes their volumes equal. Every point with distinct coordinates belongs to exactly one region; their shared boundaries have zero volume. Consequently, the region \(u\leq v\leq w\) has volume \((n-2)^3/6\).

The six possible orders of \(x,y,z\) likewise give six equal favorable regions. They exhaust the favorable outcomes without overlap, giving total favorable volume \((n-2)^3\). Hence
\[P(n)=\frac{(n-2)^3}{n^3}=\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\right)^3.\]
For \(n>2\), the positive factor \(1-2/n\) increases as \(n\) increases, so its cube also increases. Now
\[P(9)=\frac{343}{729}<\frac12\]
because \(686<729\), whereas
\[P(10)=\frac{512}{1000}>\frac12.\]
Thus every smaller positive integer fails, and the smallest possible value is \(\boxed{10}\), choice D.
